mistakes: Reading higher Kelvin as warmer. It is the opposite, and the naming convention makes this a persistent trap.
Mixing colour temperatures in one room. Two bulbs 2000 K apart will look obviously wrong together even though each looks fine alone.
Setting camera white balance to daylight indoors, which gives everything an orange cast from tungsten lighting.

qr-code-generator.intro: QR Code Generator makes a downloadable QR code from a URL, plain text, WiFi credentials, an email address, a phone number, an SMS or a contact card. Size, colours, margin and error correction are all adjustable, and the result downloads as a PNG.
how: Pick a preset (URL, WiFi, Email, Phone, SMS, Contact) or type your content directly.
Set the size between 64 and 1024 pixels.
Choose an error correction level and adjust the colours and margin.
Download the PNG.
qr-code-generator.method_title: What error correction actually buys you
method: QR codes carry redundant data so they still scan when part of the code is damaged, dirty or covered. The four levels recover roughly 7, 15, 25 and 30 percent of the code: Low, Medium, Quartile and High.

Higher correction is not free. The redundancy takes space, so the same content at High produces a denser code than at Low. Use Medium for anything on a screen, and Quartile or High for print, for stickers that will get scuffed, or when you plan to place a logo over the centre.

example.setup: Choosing a level for a printed sign:
example.result: A code that still scans with a quarter of it obscured, at the cost of a denser pattern than Low would give.

uses: Putting a link on a printed poster, menu or business card.
Sharing WiFi credentials with guests without reading out the password.
Adding a contact card to printed material.
Linking a physical product to instructions or a registration page.
mistakes: Printing too small. Below about two centimetres most phone cameras struggle, especially with a dense code.
Removing the quiet zone. The blank margin around a QR code is part of the specification and scanners need it.
Inverting the colours. Most scanners expect a dark code on a light background, and a light-on-dark code fails on many readers.
Choosing low contrast. Pale colours look nicer and scan far worse.

word-counter.intro: Word Counter reports words, characters, sentences and paragraphs as you type or paste. It is the quickest way to check a draft against a limit before you submit it.
method: Words are counted by splitting on whitespace, which is the same rule word processors use. Hyphenated compounds count as one word, and a number counts as a word.

Sentence counting looks for terminal punctuation, so abbreviations like Dr. and e.g. can inflate the count slightly. Paragraph counting splits on blank lines, which is why a document using single line breaks between paragraphs will report fewer paragraphs than you see.
uses: Checking an essay or article against a word limit before submitting.
Trimming copy to fit a fixed space in a layout.
Measuring a draft against a target length while writing.
Comparing two versions of the same piece for bloat.
mistakes: Assuming every word counter agrees. Different tools handle hyphens, numbers and em dashes differently, so check against the counter your marker or editor uses when a hard limit matters.
Counting a draft that still contains notes and placeholders.

character-counter.intro: Character Counter reports characters, bytes, Unicode code points, words, lines and spaces, and lets you set a limit so you can see how much room is left. The distinction between characters, code points and bytes is the reason this tool exists.
how: Paste or type your text.
Set a character limit to see the remaining count.
Read the separate counts for characters, bytes and code points.
character-counter.method_title: Characters, code points and bytes are three different numbers
method: For plain English they are all the same. For anything else they diverge. An accented letter is one character you see, possibly two code points, and two or more bytes in UTF-8.

Emoji are the extreme case. A single emoji is often several code points joined together, and can be four bytes or many more. That is why a tweet with emoji hits the limit sooner than the visible character count suggests, and why a database field sized in bytes overflows before it looks full.

example.setup: Common limits worth checking against:
given: 160 characters, or 70 with any non-GSM character
example.result: One emoji in an SMS drops the limit from 160 to 70, because the whole message switches encoding.

uses: Fitting a social post or a meta description inside a hard limit.
Checking whether a string will fit a database column sized in bytes.
Debugging why text that looks short is being rejected as too long.
Counting lines and spaces in fixed-format data.
mistakes: Assuming characters equal bytes. Only true for pure ASCII.
Forgetting that one non-GSM character reprices an entire SMS.
Counting trailing whitespace out of the total. Most systems count it.

text-statistics.intro: Text Statistics runs a deeper analysis than a word count: readability scores, vocabulary richness, sentence complexity, and paragraph structure, all from a block of pasted text.
method: Vocabulary richness is the ratio of unique words to total words. A low ratio means heavy repetition, which is sometimes deliberate and often a sign of a draft that needs editing.

Sentence complexity comes mostly from average sentence length. Long sentences are not automatically bad, but a document where every sentence is long is tiring to read, and one where they are all short reads as choppy. The useful signal is variation, not a single target number.
uses: Diagnosing why a draft feels heavy without being able to say why.
Checking that writing matches the reading level of its audience.
Finding paragraphs that have quietly grown to twice the length of their neighbours.
Comparing your own writing across pieces to spot habits.
mistakes: Optimising for a score. Readability formulas measure sentence and word length, not clarity, and you can score well while making no sense.
Applying general readability targets to technical writing, where necessary terminology is long by nature.

reading-time-calculator.intro: Reading Time Calculator estimates how long a piece takes to read, with an adjustable reading speed so you can model a fast skim or a careful read.
how: Paste your text.
Set the reading speed in words per minute.
Read the estimated time.
method: Reading time is the word count divided by a words-per-minute rate. The whole estimate hinges on which rate you pick, which is why the tool lets you change it rather than hiding a fixed assumption.

Adult silent reading of general prose runs about 200 to 250 words per minute. Careful reading of technical material is much slower, often 100 to 150. Reading aloud is slower still, around 130 to 150, which is the figure to use for a script or a speech.

example.setup: A 1,500 word article at different rates:
example.result: The same text is a 5 minute read or an 11 minute talk depending entirely on the rate you assume.

uses: Adding an honest reading time estimate to an article.
Timing a speech or a video script before you record it.
Checking whether a document fits the attention you can realistically expect.
Planning how much material a training session needs.
mistakes: Using a silent reading rate for a script. Speaking is much slower and the estimate will be badly short.
Ignoring figures, tables and code. Readers slow right down or stop at them, and word count does not capture that.

reading-level-analyzer.intro: Reading Level Analyzer scores text with the Flesch reading ease and Flesch-Kincaid grade level formulas, giving you a US school grade estimate for how demanding a piece is.
reading-level-analyzer.method_title: The formulas, and what they actually measure
method: Flesch reading ease is 206.835 minus 1.015 times the average words per sentence, minus 84.6 times the average syllables per word. Higher is easier. Flesch-Kincaid grade level rearranges the same two inputs to output a US grade instead.

Both formulas only see two things: how long your sentences are and how many syllables your words have. They know nothing about logic, structure or whether a sentence makes sense. A well-argued paragraph and a grammatically identical piece of nonsense score the same.

example.setup: How the scale reads:
example.result: General audience writing usually targets 60 to 70, the range most newspapers sit in.

uses: Checking that public-facing writing is accessible.
Meeting a plain-language requirement for a policy or a form.
Comparing a draft against published writing you consider clear.
Spotting sections where sentence length has crept up.
mistakes: Chasing a lower grade by chopping every sentence short. That produces choppy writing that scores well and reads badly.
Applying the formulas to technical documents. Necessary domain terms are long and the score punishes them unfairly.
Treating the grade as a verdict on quality. It measures surface complexity only.

word-frequency.intro: Word Frequency Analyzer ranks the most common words in a block of text, with optional stop word removal, case folding, and a configurable list length. Results export to CSV.
how: Paste your text.
Turn on Remove stop words to hide the, and, of and their kin.
Set case-insensitive if The and the should count together.
Choose how many results to show, and export to CSV if you need them elsewhere.
method: Without filtering, the top of any English frequency list is always the same: the, of, and, to, a. Those function words carry grammar rather than meaning, so they tell you nothing about the text.
Removing them surfaces the words that actually characterise the document. That is the same first step used in search indexing and text classification, for exactly the same reason.
uses: Finding the words you overuse in your own writing.
Pulling likely keywords out of a document.
Comparing two pieces of writing by their vocabulary.
Checking whether an article actually covers the topic it claims to.
mistakes: Reading frequency as importance. A word repeated because of a formatting quirk will top the list without meaning anything.
Leaving case sensitivity on when you did not mean to, which splits The and the into two entries.
Removing stop words when studying writing style. For that question the function words are the interesting part.

typing-test.intro: Typing Test measures words per minute and accuracy over 30, 60 or 120 seconds, with word lists, quotes, or your own custom text to type.
how: Choose a mode: Words, Quotes, or Custom text.
Pick a duration of 30, 60 or 120 seconds.
Start typing. Errors are marked as you go.
Read your WPM and accuracy at the end.
method: A word in typing measurement is defined as five characters, including spaces. Your gross WPM is the number of characters typed divided by five, divided by the minutes elapsed. That standard exists so that typing hello and typing internationalisation are scored proportionately.

Net WPM subtracts errors. This is why accuracy matters more than raw speed: at 90 percent accuracy you are spending a tenth of your effort producing text that has to be fixed, and in real work the correction costs more time than the typing saved.

example.setup: Working out a score:
example.result: 60 WPM gross. Average adult typing is about 40 WPM, and professional typists run 70 to 90.

uses: Measuring a baseline before practising.
Tracking improvement over weeks.
Practising on your own text, which is more useful than random word lists.
Preparing for a job that tests typing speed.
mistakes: Practising speed at the expense of accuracy. Speed built on errors does not transfer to real work.
Testing for 30 seconds only. Short tests flatter you, because everyone can sprint briefly.
Looking at the keyboard. It caps your ceiling permanently, however fast you get in the short term.

text-diff.intro: Text Diff compares two blocks of text and highlights what changed, line by line, with options to ignore case and leading whitespace.
how: Paste the original into the first box and the new version into the second.
Turn on Ignore case or Ignore leading whitespace if those differences are noise for your purpose.
Press Compare and read the highlighted result.
method: A diff finds the longest sequence of lines the two versions share, then reports everything else as added or removed. Working line by line is what makes the output readable, which is why version control systems do the same.
The consequence is that changing one word marks the whole line as changed. That is not a flaw, it is the trade: a character-level diff is more precise and much harder to read at a glance.
uses: Finding what changed between two drafts of a document.
Checking a config file against a known-good version.
Comparing exported data before and after a process ran.
Spotting an unintended edit in copy you have handed round for review.
mistakes: Comparing files with different line endings without normalising first. Windows CRLF against Unix LF makes every single line look changed.
Leaving whitespace sensitivity on when comparing indented code or data, which buries the real changes in noise.
Diffing reformatted text. If a reflow changed every line break, the diff cannot tell you anything useful.

sort-lines-alpha.intro: Sort Lines Alphabetically puts any list into A to Z or Z to A order. Paste the list, pick a direction, copy the result.
how: Paste your list, one item per line.
Choose A to Z or Z to A.
Copy the sorted result.
sort-lines-alpha.method_title: Why sorted output sometimes looks wrong
method: Naive alphabetical sorting compares character codes, and in that scheme every uppercase letter comes before every lowercase one. Z sorts before a, so a mixed-case list can look shuffled rather than sorted.

Numbers inside text cause the other surprise. Character-by-character comparison puts item10 before item2, because it compares the 1 against the 2 and stops there. That is correct lexicographic ordering and almost never what you wanted.

example.setup: A mixed list sorted by character code:
example.result: All capitalised entries sort ahead of all lowercase ones, which surprises most people the first time.

uses: Alphabetising a list of names, tags or references.
Putting an import or export file in a predictable order.
Making two lists comparable before diffing them.
Tidying a bibliography or glossary.
mistakes: Sorting a list with inconsistent capitalisation and expecting dictionary order.
Sorting numbered items and expecting numeric order. Ten will land next to one.
Sorting data that has a header line, which gets sorted into the middle with everything else.

sort-lines-length.intro: Sort Lines by Length orders a list by how many characters each line has, shortest first or longest first.
how: Paste your list, one item per line.
Choose shortest to longest or longest to shortest.
Copy the result.
sort-lines-length.method_title: What length sorting is good for
method: Length is a proxy for several things that are otherwise hard to spot. In a list of records, unusually short lines are often truncated or empty, and unusually long ones often contain a delimiter that failed to split.
Lines of equal length keep their original relative order, so the sort is stable. That means you can sort by length and still see the input sequence within each length group.
uses: Finding malformed rows in exported data by spotting outliers at both ends.
Ordering a list for visual layout, where a length ramp reads better.
Finding the longest entry to size a column or a field.
Spotting truncated values in a dump.
mistakes: Assuming character length equals visual width. In a proportional font an i and a w are very different widths.
Counting trailing whitespace as content. Trim first if the trailing spaces are not meaningful.

dedupe-lines.intro: Duplicate Line Remover strips repeated lines from a list, leaving one of each. The original order of the first occurrences is preserved.
how: Paste your list.
The deduplicated result appears immediately.
Copy it out.
method: Two lines are duplicates only if they match exactly. A trailing space, a different capitalisation, or a stray tab makes two lines distinct even though they look identical on screen.

That is why deduplication so often appears not to work. The fix is to trim whitespace first, and to normalise case if case is not meaningful in your data. Running the trim tool before this one solves the large majority of cases.
uses: Cleaning a mailing list or a list of IDs before import.
Removing repeats after merging two lists together.
Finding the distinct set of values in a column pasted from a spreadsheet.
Tidying a tag or keyword list.
mistakes: Not trimming first. Invisible trailing whitespace is the single most common reason duplicates survive.
Ignoring case differences when they are not meaningful, leaving Apple and apple as two entries.
Deduplicating data where the repeats were meaningful, such as counts or transaction records.

trim-lines.intro: Line Trimmer removes leading and trailing whitespace from every line, leaving the content and the line structure intact.
how: Paste your text.
The trimmed result appears immediately.
Copy it out.
trim-lines.method_title: Why trailing whitespace causes so much trouble
method: Trailing spaces are invisible, and almost every system treats them as content. They break exact-match comparisons, defeat deduplication, corrupt lookup keys, and produce mystifying bugs where two apparently identical values are not equal.
Trimming removes spaces and tabs from both ends of each line. It does not touch whitespace inside a line, so words stay separated and internal formatting survives.
uses: Cleaning data copied out of a PDF or a web page, which routinely carries stray spaces.
Preparing a list for deduplication or comparison.
Fixing indentation that came along with pasted text.
Normalising values before importing into a database.
mistakes: Trimming code where leading whitespace is the indentation and carries meaning. Python in particular will break.
Assuming trimming fixes non-breaking spaces. A non-breaking space is a different character and often survives a trim.

remove-empty-lines.intro: Empty Line Remover deletes blank lines from a block of text, closing up the gaps and leaving the content lines in order.
how: Paste your text.
Blank lines are removed immediately.
Copy the compacted result.
method: A truly empty line contains nothing. A line containing only spaces or a tab looks identical on screen but is not empty, and a naive removal leaves it behind.
That is the usual explanation when gaps survive the process. Trimming the text first turns whitespace-only lines into genuinely empty ones, after which they are removed cleanly.
uses: Compacting a list that picked up gaps when it was copied.
Cleaning text pasted out of a PDF, where double spacing is common.
Preparing a list where each line must be a real record.
Tightening output before pasting it somewhere space-constrained.
mistakes: Removing blank lines from Markdown, where a blank line is what separates paragraphs. Strip them and the whole document becomes one block.
Doing this to poetry or formatted text where the spacing is deliberate.

reverse-lines.intro: Reverse Lines flips the order of lines in a block of text so the last line becomes the first. The lines themselves are unchanged.
how: Paste your text.
The reversed order appears immediately.
Copy the result.
method: This reverses the sequence of lines. It does not reverse the characters within a line, which is a different operation and rarely what people want.
The most common real use is log files. Most logs append newest entries at the bottom, so reversing gives you newest first without needing a tool that understands timestamps.
uses: Reading a log file newest first.
Flipping a chronological list into reverse chronological order.
Reversing a ranked list to run from lowest to highest.
Undoing a reversal someone else applied.
mistakes: Expecting character reversal. Line order and character order are separate things.
Reversing text that has a header row, which ends up at the bottom.

join-lines.intro: Join Lines collapses multiple lines into a single line, separated by whatever delimiter you choose: a comma, a space, a pipe, or anything else.
how: Paste your list, one item per line.
Set the separator you want between items.
Copy the joined result.
method: The separator has to be a character that does not appear inside your data. Joining a list of full names with a comma is fine until one entry is Smith, John, at which point the result is ambiguous and cannot be split back.

Comma and space suit prose. Pipe or tab suit data, because they rarely occur naturally. If your values might contain the separator, they need quoting, which is exactly the problem CSV formats exist to solve.
uses: Turning a column copied from a spreadsheet into a comma-separated list.
Building an SQL IN clause from a list of IDs.
Converting a list into a single line for a config value or a command argument.
Making a list of tags into a single field.
mistakes: Using a separator that appears in the data, producing output that cannot be reliably split again.
Forgetting that the join removes the line structure permanently. Keep the original if you need it back.

split-text.intro: Split Text breaks a block of text into chunks by character count, word count, or a delimiter you specify.
how: Paste your text.
Choose how to split: by characters, by words, or on a delimiter.
Set the size or the delimiter and copy the chunks.
method: Splitting by delimiter is the right choice when the text has real structure, such as comma-separated values or paragraphs separated by blank lines. The boundaries already exist and you are just honouring them.

Splitting by character or word count is for when you need to fit a limit, such as breaking a long message into posts. Character splitting can cut a word in half, so word splitting is usually kinder to the reader even though the chunks come out slightly uneven.
uses: Breaking a long message into pieces that fit a character limit.
Splitting a delimited string back into records.
Chunking text for processing in fixed batches.
Dividing a long document into sections of even length.
mistakes: Splitting on a comma when the data contains quoted commas. That needs a real CSV parser, not a plain split.
Splitting by character count for anything a human will read, which chops words mid-syllable.

word-wrap.intro: Word Wrap Formatter rewraps text at a column width you choose, with hard or soft wrapping and the option to preserve blank lines.
how: Paste your text and set the wrap column.
Choose hard wrap if long words should be broken rather than allowed to overhang.
Turn on Preserve blank lines to keep paragraph breaks.
Press Wrap and copy the output.
word-wrap.method_title: Hard wrap, soft wrap, and why 72 columns
method: Soft wrapping breaks between words, so a word longer than the column width overhangs. Hard wrapping breaks inside the word to guarantee no line exceeds the limit, which matters for fixed-width output but looks worse.

The traditional widths come from real constraints. Punched cards were 80 columns, and email settled on 72 so that quoted replies could add their angle brackets without pushing past 80. Both conventions survive in plain-text formats and commit messages.
uses: Formatting a git commit message body to the conventional width.
Preparing plain-text email that will not wrap raggedly in someone else's client.
Fitting text into a fixed-width terminal display.
Reflowing a paragraph after editing broke the line lengths.
mistakes: Hard wrapping prose that will be displayed in a variable-width window. The reader's own wrapping will fight your line breaks.
Wrapping code or Markdown tables, where the line structure is meaningful.
Wrapping at 80 when the content will be quoted in a reply, which pushes it over.

slugify-text.intro: Slugify Text converts any string into a clean, URL-safe slug: lowercase, hyphen-separated, with punctuation and accents removed.
how: Paste your title or phrase.
The slug appears immediately.
Copy it into your URL, filename or ID.
slugify-text.method_title: What slugifying does, step by step
method: The text is lowercased, accented characters are folded to their plain equivalents, punctuation is stripped, and runs of whitespace become single hyphens. Leading and trailing hyphens are removed.
Lowercase matters more than people expect. URL paths are case-sensitive on most servers, so Page and page are different addresses. Forcing lowercase removes an entire class of broken link.

example.setup: A messy title becoming a slug:
example.result: cafe-reviews-the-10-best

uses: Generating a URL path from an article title.
Creating safe filenames from user-supplied names.
Making stable IDs for anchors and fragments.
Normalising a title into a database key.
mistakes: Changing a slug after publishing. The old URL breaks unless you add a redirect, and any accumulated links point at nothing.
Letting slugs get long. Search results truncate them and they become unreadable.
Assuming accent folding suits every language. Some scripts have no sensible ASCII equivalent and need transliteration rules of their own.

smart-quotes-converter.intro: Smart Quotes Converter switches between curly typographic quotes and straight ASCII quotes, in either direction. It is the fix for text that has been through a word processor and is now breaking something.
how: Paste your text.
Convert curly quotes to straight, or straight to curly.
Copy the result.
method: Straight quotes are the ASCII characters at code points 34 and 39. Curly quotes are separate Unicode characters: the left and right single marks and the left and right double marks. They look better in prose and are what typesetting has always used.

The trouble starts when text is pasted into something that expects ASCII. Code will not compile, because a curly quote is not a string delimiter. CSV files break. Search fails, because a search for don't will not match don with a curly apostrophe. Word processors substitute curly quotes automatically, which is why this problem usually arrives without anyone choosing it.
uses: Fixing code that was pasted through a word processor or a chat client.
Cleaning text before importing it as CSV or JSON.
Converting straight quotes to curly for print or a designed layout.
Making search and comparison work on text with mixed quote styles.
mistakes: Converting code comments and strings indiscriminately. Straight to curly will break code that currently works.
Forgetting apostrophes. The curly right single quote is the same character used for apostrophes, so it appears far more often than quotation marks do.
Assuming a find and replace handles it. There are four curly characters, not one.

nato-alphabet.intro: NATO Alphabet Converter turns text into the NATO phonetic alphabet, spelling each letter as Alfa, Bravo, Charlie and so on, so it can be read aloud without being misheard.
how: Type or paste the text you need to spell out.
Read the phonetic version, and copy it if you need it in writing.
method: The alphabet was chosen after extensive testing to find words that stay distinguishable over poor radio links and across accents. The whole point is that no two code words sound alike, even when the signal is bad.

Two spellings are deliberately irregular. Alfa is spelled with an f rather than ph, and Juliett has a double t, both so that speakers of languages where ph or a final t is silent still pronounce them correctly. They are not typos.

example.setup: Spelling a booking reference over the phone:
example.result: Unambiguous where B and V, or K and A, would otherwise be confused.

uses: Reading a reference number, postcode or serial over the phone.
Confirming a spelling in a noisy environment.
Aviation, maritime and emergency radio use, where it is standard.
Dictating an email address or a password reset code without errors.
mistakes: Inventing your own words. A for Apple works until the other person expects Alfa and mishears.
Spelling Alfa as Alpha and Juliett with one t. Both are officially spelled the irregular way for a reason.
Using it for letters that are already unambiguous, which slows the exchange down without helping.

markdown-to-html.intro: Markdown to HTML converts Markdown into clean HTML with a live preview, so you can see the rendered result and copy the markup side by side.
how: Paste or type your Markdown.
Switch between HTML and Preview to see the output either way.
Copy the HTML when it looks right.
method: Markdown was designed by John Gruber in 2004 with one goal: a plain-text format readable as-is, that converts cleanly to HTML. That is why the syntax mirrors how people already marked up plain-text email, with asterisks for emphasis and hashes for headings.

There is no single Markdown. CommonMark is the strict specification, and GitHub Flavored Markdown adds tables, task lists and strikethrough. Two converters can legitimately produce different HTML from the same input where the original spec was ambiguous.
uses: Turning notes into HTML for a page or an email.
Checking how your Markdown will render before committing it.
Producing HTML for a CMS that does not accept Markdown.
Learning what each piece of Markdown syntax becomes.
mistakes: Expecting tables to work everywhere. Tables are a GitHub Flavored extension, not part of original Markdown.
Relying on a single line break for a new line. Markdown needs a blank line for a new paragraph, or two trailing spaces for a line break.
Indenting text by four spaces without meaning to, which turns it into a code block.

markdown-table-maker.intro: Markdown Table Maker builds a properly formatted Markdown table from plain text or CSV, handling the column alignment and the separator row so you do not have to line up pipes by hand.
how: Paste your data as plain text or CSV.
The formatted Markdown table appears below.
Copy it into your document.
markdown-table-maker.method_title: How a Markdown table is structured
method: A table is three parts: a header row of cells separated by pipes, a separator row of dashes, and the data rows. The separator row is what tells the parser this is a table at all, and it must have the same number of columns as the header.

Alignment is set with colons in that separator row. A colon on the left aligns left, on the right aligns right, and on both sides centres the column. Without a colon the renderer picks its own default.

example.setup: The minimum structure a table needs:
example.result: Name aligns left, Score aligns right. Getting the separator row wrong is why most hand-written tables fail to render.

uses: Building a table for a README or a wiki page without counting pipes.
Converting a spreadsheet column selection into Markdown.
Reformatting a table someone pasted in as loose text.
Producing documentation tables that stay readable in the raw file.
mistakes: Mismatching the column count between the header and the separator row, which stops it rendering as a table at all.
Using a pipe character inside a cell without escaping it, which splits the cell in two.
Assuming tables work in every Markdown renderer. They are an extension, and some strict parsers ignore them.

markdown-cheatsheet.intro: Markdown Cheatsheet is a complete syntax reference with live examples: headings, emphasis, links, images, lists, code, blockquotes, tables and more, each shown as source and as rendered output.
method: Most of Markdown is six or seven patterns. Hashes for headings, asterisks or underscores for emphasis, square brackets and parentheses for links, hyphens or numbers for lists, backticks for code, and a greater-than sign for quotes.

The rules that catch people out are about blank lines. A paragraph ends at a blank line, a list needs one before it in many parsers, and a fenced code block needs its opening and closing fences on their own lines.
uses: Looking up syntax you use rarely, like reference-style links or nested lists.
Learning Markdown by seeing source and output together.
Checking which features are core Markdown and which are extensions.
Keeping a reference open while writing documentation.
notes: Every example shows the raw syntax next to the rendered result.
Covers both core Markdown and the common GitHub Flavored extensions.

markdown-link-cleaner.intro: Markdown Link Cleaner takes messy pasted links and turns them into tidy Markdown, optionally stripping tracking parameters, fetching the real page titles, and formatting the result as a bulleted or numbered list.
how: Paste your links, one per line or mixed into text.
Turn on Strip UTM tracking parameters to remove campaign junk from the URLs.
Optionally fetch live page titles, which takes longer but produces properly named links.
Choose a list format and copy the output.
markdown-link-cleaner.method_title: What UTM parameters are and why to remove them
method: UTM parameters are the query fields marketers append to track where a click came from: utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, utm_term and utm_content. They are added by the sender, mean nothing to the destination page, and often make a URL two or three times longer than it needs to be.
Stripping them almost always leaves a working link to the same page, and it stops you passing someone else's campaign tracking on to your readers when you share a link.
uses: Turning a pile of copied URLs into a clean reference list.
Cleaning links before publishing them, so readers do not inherit tracking parameters.
Building a linked bibliography with real page titles rather than bare URLs.
Tidying links pasted out of a newsletter, which are usually the worst offenders.
mistakes: Stripping query parameters indiscriminately. Some parameters are functional and the page will break without them, so only tracking parameters should go.
Fetching titles for a long list and expecting it to be instant. Each one is a separate network request.
notes: Fetching live page titles requires a network request per link, so it is slower than the offline options.

markdown-list-cleaner.intro: Markdown List Cleaner normalises messy lists: inconsistent bullet characters, ragged indentation, and numbering that has drifted out of sequence.
how: Paste your list.
The cleaned version appears immediately.
Copy it back into your document.
method: Markdown accepts hyphen, asterisk and plus as bullet characters, and mixing them within one list can split it into several lists in some parsers. Standardising on one character avoids the whole problem.

Indentation is the other common failure. Nesting requires a consistent indent, and a list pasted from another editor often arrives with a mix of tabs and spaces that renders as a code block instead of a nested list.
uses: Fixing a list pasted from a document or an email.
Standardising bullet characters across a file.
Repairing nesting that renders wrongly.
Renumbering an ordered list that has gone out of sequence.
mistakes: Mixing tabs and spaces for indentation, which is the single most common cause of a list rendering as code.
Assuming ordered list numbers must be sequential in the source. Most parsers renumber automatically, so 1. 1. 1. renders as 1. 2. 3.

markdown-frontmatter.intro: Frontmatter Generator builds the YAML or TOML metadata block that sits at the top of a post in a static site generator, with fields for title, date, slug, author and tags, plus any custom fields you add.
how: Fill in the title, date, author and tags. The slug is generated from the title automatically.
Add any custom fields your site needs.
Switch between YAML and TOML output.
Copy the block to the top of your post file.
markdown-frontmatter.method_title: YAML or TOML, and where each is used
method: Frontmatter is a metadata block at the very top of a content file, separated from the body by delimiters. YAML frontmatter is fenced by three hyphens and is the default in Jekyll, Eleventy, Astro and most of the ecosystem. TOML frontmatter is fenced by three plus signs and is common in Hugo.

The format has to match what your generator expects, and the opening delimiter must be the first line of the file. A single blank line above it and the generator will treat the whole block as body text.

example.setup: A minimal YAML block:
example.result: Three hyphens, the fields, three hyphens, then the post body. The opening delimiter must be line one.

uses: Starting a new blog post with correctly formed metadata.
Adding a custom field consistently across posts.
Switching a site between YAML and TOML conventions.
Avoiding the YAML quoting errors that break a build.
mistakes: Leaving a colon unquoted inside a title. YAML reads it as a key separator and the build fails.
Putting a blank line before the opening delimiter, which stops it being recognised as frontmatter.
Using the wrong date format. Most generators want ISO 8601, and a locale-formatted date will either fail or sort wrongly.

lorem-ipsum-generator.intro: Lorem Ipsum Generator produces placeholder text by paragraph, sentence or word count, with the option to open with the traditional Lorem ipsum line.
how: Choose paragraphs, sentences or words.
Set the count.
Decide whether to start with the classic opening line.
Generate and copy.
method: The text is scrambled Latin taken from Cicero's De Finibus Bonorum et Malorum, written in 45 BC. It has been used as typesetting filler since at least the 1500s, when a printer scrambled a passage to make a type specimen book.

It survives because it is deliberately meaningless. Readable placeholder text pulls attention to the words, and a client reviewing a layout starts editing the copy instead of assessing the design. Latin-looking nonsense with roughly English word-length distribution keeps the focus on the layout.
uses: Filling a design mockup before real copy exists.
Testing how a layout handles different text lengths.
Checking line height, measure and typography with realistic word shapes.
Populating a database or a template for testing.
mistakes: Shipping it to production. Lorem ipsum appearing on a live site is a classic and very visible mistake.
Using it to test text that will be much shorter or longer in reality, which hides layout problems until launch.
Forgetting it is Latin-shaped. If your real content is in a language with much longer words or a different script, it will not stress the layout the same way.

lorem-ipsum-blocks.intro: Lorem Ipsum Blocks generates placeholder text in five different voices: classic Lorem Ipsum, random English, hipster ipsum, office speak, and nature and science vocabulary.
how: Choose a style.
Set how many paragraphs and how many sentences each.
Regenerate until you have something that fits, then copy.
lorem-ipsum-blocks.method_title: Why the style of placeholder matters
method: Classic Lorem Ipsum is deliberately unreadable, which keeps reviewers focused on layout. That is a strength when presenting a design and a weakness when you need to know how real English will look, because Latin word lengths and letter frequencies differ from English.

English-based placeholder gives a more honest preview of line breaks, hyphenation and rag. Themed styles like office speak or nature vocabulary are useful when the design is for a specific context and you want the texture to feel right without writing real copy.
uses: Presenting a layout where the placeholder should feel plausible rather than obviously fake.
Testing typography with realistic English word lengths.
Filling a themed mockup where Latin would look out of place.
Generating varied test content for a template.
mistakes: Using readable English placeholder in a client review, where it invites copy edits instead of design feedback.
Leaving joke placeholder text in a file that later ships.

text-case-converter.intro: Text Case Converter switches text between uppercase, lowercase, title case and sentence case.
how: Paste your text.
Choose the case you want.
Copy the result.
text-case-converter.method_title: Title case is not one rule
method: Uppercase, lowercase and sentence case are mechanical. Title case is not, because style guides disagree about which words to leave lowercase. Most lowercase short articles, conjunctions and prepositions (a, an, the, and, of, in) unless they are the first or last word, but the length threshold for prepositions varies between guides.

Case conversion also has language traps. In Turkish, the uppercase of a dotless i is a dotless I, and applying English rules produces the wrong letter. Any conversion done for machine comparison rather than display should use a locale-independent fold.
uses: Fixing a heading that was typed in all caps.
Normalising imported data where capitalisation is inconsistent.
Converting a title to your publication's house style.
Rescuing text from a caps lock accident.
mistakes: Applying title case to a sentence and getting proper nouns wrong. No automatic rule knows that iPhone and eBay keep their lowercase first letter.
Uppercasing text for comparison instead of using a case fold, which breaks on several languages.
Sentence-casing text containing acronyms, which turns NASA into Nasa.

tag-stripper.intro: Tag Stripper removes HTML and XML tags, Markdown formatting, or both, leaving plain text. It can also decode HTML entities and collapse the extra whitespace that stripping leaves behind.
how: Paste your marked-up text.
Tick what to strip: HTML/XML tags, Markdown formatting, or both.
Optionally decode entities and collapse whitespace.
Press Strip and copy the output.
tag-stripper.method_title: Why stripping leaves a mess without the extra options
method: Removing tags alone gives you text littered with entities like & and  , because those are not tags. Decoding entities turns them back into the characters they represent.

Stripping also leaves whitespace behind. Block-level tags were providing the visual separation, and once they are gone you get either everything jammed together or long runs of blank lines. Collapsing whitespace fixes that, which is why these three options belong together.
uses: Getting plain text out of a copied web page for use elsewhere.
Extracting readable content from an HTML email.
Converting Markdown to plain text for a system that cannot render it.
Cleaning scraped content before analysing it.
mistakes: Stripping tags from content you need to keep structured. This is a one-way operation and the structure is not recoverable.
Forgetting to decode entities, leaving & scattered through the output.
Using tag stripping as a security measure. Sanitising untrusted HTML properly needs a real parser, not a strip.

html-entity-encoder.intro: HTML Entity Encoder converts characters that have special meaning in HTML into their entity form, so they display as text instead of being interpreted as markup.
how: Paste the text you want to encode.
The encoded output appears immediately.
Copy it into your HTML.
html-entity-encoder.method_title: The five that matter, and the order they go in
method: Five characters need encoding in HTML: ampersand becomes &, less-than becomes <, greater-than becomes >, double quote becomes ", and single quote becomes '.

The ampersand must be encoded first. If you encode the angle brackets before the ampersands, you then encode the ampersands inside the entities you just created, and < becomes &lt;, which displays as literal text rather than a less-than sign. Getting this order wrong is the classic double-encoding bug.

example.setup: Encoding a snippet so it displays as text:
example.result: <b>Tom & Jerry</b> renders on the page as the literal tag text.

uses: Displaying code examples on a web page without them being parsed as markup.
Escaping user-supplied text before inserting it into HTML.
Fixing content where a stray angle bracket is breaking the layout.
Preparing text for an XML document, which has the same rules.
mistakes: Encoding in the wrong order and producing double-encoded output.
Encoding text that is already encoded, which has the same effect.
Treating entity encoding as complete XSS protection. It is the right tool for text content, but attribute values and inline script contexts need their own escaping rules.

html-entity-decoder.intro: HTML Entity Decoder turns entities like &, < and ' back into the characters they represent, recovering readable plain text.
how: Paste text containing HTML entities.
The decoded output appears immediately.
Copy the plain text.
method: Entities come in two forms. Named entities like & and   are readable but only a fixed set exists. Numeric entities like ' and ' reference a Unicode code point directly in decimal or hexadecimal, and can represent any character.

Decoding runs the encoding order in reverse, so ampersands are decoded last. Decode them first and &lt; turns into < and then into a real less-than sign, which is one level of decoding too many and can reintroduce markup you did not intend.
uses: Reading text extracted from HTML source or an API response.
Cleaning content that has been double-encoded somewhere in a pipeline.
Recovering plain text from a scraped page.
Debugging why a page displays & instead of an ampersand.
mistakes: Decoding untrusted content and then inserting it into a page, which can reintroduce active markup. Decode for display as text, not for injection into HTML.
Decoding repeatedly until nothing changes. One pass is usually correct, and repeated passes can turn escaped content into live markup.

url-extractor.intro: URL Extractor pulls every link out of a block of text or HTML and lists them, so you can get a clean set of URLs from messy source material.
how: Paste text, HTML, or anything containing links.
The extracted URLs are listed below.
Copy the list.
url-extractor.method_title: Why URL extraction is harder than it looks
method: Finding URLs by pattern means deciding where one ends, and that is genuinely ambiguous. A URL at the end of a sentence is usually not meant to include the full stop, but a full stop is legal inside a URL path, so any rule will occasionally be wrong.

Closing brackets have the same problem. A link inside parentheses usually should not include the closing bracket, but Wikipedia URLs legitimately contain them. Extraction tools apply heuristics that are right most of the time rather than a rule that is right always.
uses: Collecting every link from a page or an email for review.
Building a list of references from a document.
Auditing which external sites a piece of content points to.
Pulling links out of a chat export or a plain-text file.
mistakes: Assuming the list is exhaustive. Links built by JavaScript at runtime do not exist in the source text.
Not checking for trailing punctuation before using the URLs.
Extracting from rendered text rather than HTML, which loses the href of any link whose visible text is not the URL.

email-extractor.intro: Email Extractor pulls every email address out of a block of text and lists them cleanly.
how: Paste text containing email addresses.
The extracted addresses appear below.
Copy the list.
email-extractor.method_title: Why no pattern matches every valid address
method: The formal definition of an email address in RFC 5322 permits quoted strings, comments, and characters most people never see, and a regular expression that matches it correctly runs to thousands of characters. No practical tool implements it.

So extraction uses a pragmatic pattern that matches the addresses that actually occur. It will miss exotic but technically valid forms, and the only way to truly validate an address is to send mail to it.
uses: Collecting contact addresses from a document you have been given.
Auditing a page or a file for exposed addresses before publishing it.
Pulling addresses out of a pasted email header block.
Building a distribution list from meeting notes.
mistakes: Treating extraction as validation. A well-formed address can still be undeliverable.
Missing addresses that have been obfuscated as name at domain dot com, which is deliberate and will not match.
Using extracted addresses for unsolicited mail, which is unlawful in most jurisdictions.

number-extractor.intro: Number Extractor pulls all the numbers out of a block of text, which is the quickest way to get figures out of a report, an invoice, or a paragraph of prose into a usable list.
how: Paste text containing numbers.
The extracted numbers appear below.
Copy them out.
method: Extraction has to decide about decimal points, thousands separators and signs. In most of the English-speaking world a comma groups thousands and a full stop is the decimal point, but much of Europe reverses the two, so 1.234 is a thousand-something in Berlin and one-point-something in Boston.
That ambiguity cannot be resolved from the digits alone, only from context. Check the output against the source when the text might have come from a different locale.
uses: Getting figures out of a pasted report into a spreadsheet.
Extracting quantities or prices from a block of prose.
Pulling reference or order numbers out of an email.
Collecting measurements from notes.
mistakes: Assuming the locale. A comma might be a decimal separator, and the difference is a factor of a thousand.
Losing the association between a number and what it referred to. Extraction gives you values without labels.
Extracting from text with phone numbers or dates mixed in, which produces figures that are not quantities at all.

add-line-numbers.intro: Add Line Numbers prefixes every line of a block of text with its number, which is what you need when you are about to talk to someone about specific lines.
how: Paste your text.
The numbered version appears immediately.
Copy it out.
method: Numbered lines give you a shared reference. Saying line 47 is unambiguous in a way that quoting a snippet is not, particularly when the same text appears more than once in a file.

Numbers are padded so they align, which keeps the content in a straight column. Without padding, the jump from line 9 to line 10 shifts every following line one character to the right and makes the text harder to scan.
uses: Preparing a code or config excerpt for a code review comment.
Referring to specific lines in a document during a discussion.
Producing numbered output for a bug report.
Making a long list easier to count and reference.
mistakes: Numbering text that will be pasted back into a file or a compiler. The numbers become content and break it.
Numbering before removing blank lines, which numbers the gaps too.

strip-line-numbers.intro: Strip Line Numbers removes leading line numbers from text, which is what you need after copying a code sample out of a documentation page or a terminal that numbers its output.
how: Paste the numbered text.
The numbers are removed and the content is left intact.
Copy the clean result.
strip-line-numbers.method_title: The formats it has to handle
method: Numbering appears in several conventions: a bare number and a space, a number and a colon, a number and a pipe, or a right-aligned number padded with spaces. All of them have to go while leaving the code's own indentation untouched.
That last part is the difficult bit. Stripping too aggressively takes the leading whitespace with the number, and for Python or YAML that destroys the meaning of the file.
uses: Cleaning a code sample copied from documentation or a blog post.
Removing numbering from terminal output before reusing it.
Recovering usable code from a screenshot transcription.
Undoing numbering you added earlier.
mistakes: Stripping numbers from content where the leading numbers are the data, such as a numbered list or a CSV whose first column is an ID.
Losing indentation along with the numbers, which breaks indentation-sensitive languages.

add-prefix-suffix.intro: Add Prefix / Suffix puts custom text at the start of every line, the end of every line, or both. It turns a plain list into formatted output in one step.
how: Paste your list, one item per line.
Enter a prefix, a suffix, or both.
Copy the result.
method: Most uses are about converting a plain list into some syntax. Wrapping each line in quotes and a comma turns a column of values into an array literal. Adding a hyphen and a space turns it into a Markdown list. Adding a tag turns it into HTML.
It is the fastest path from data you have to the format something else demands, without writing a script or reaching for a spreadsheet formula.

example.setup: Turning a list of IDs into a SQL clause:
example.result: 'A123', which pasted together forms the body of an IN clause.

uses: Quoting a list of values for code or SQL.
Turning a plain list into Markdown bullets.
Wrapping lines in HTML tags.
Adding a common path or domain to a list of filenames.
mistakes: Forgetting the last line still gets the suffix, so a trailing comma may need removing by hand.
Adding quotes to values that already contain quotes, which needs escaping rather than wrapping.

text-alignment.intro: Text Alignment formats text to a fixed column width, aligned left, right, centred or justified, with the option to preserve paragraph breaks.
how: Paste your text and set the column width.
Choose left, right, centre or justify.
Turn on Preserve paragraph breaks to keep the structure.
Copy the formatted output.
text-alignment.method_title: How justification works in plain text
method: Left, right and centre alignment just add padding spaces on one side or both. Justification is different: it stretches the gaps between words so each line reaches the full width on both edges.

This only works in a monospaced context, because it counts characters rather than measuring pixel widths. Paste justified plain text into a proportional font and the careful spacing collapses into an uneven mess.
uses: Formatting text for a terminal, a code comment, or a README.
Producing fixed-width output for a system that expects it.
Centring a heading in a plain-text document or an ASCII banner.
Making a plain-text email look deliberately laid out.
mistakes: Justifying text that will be displayed in a proportional font, where the added spaces make it worse rather than better.
Choosing too narrow a width, which forces large gaps between words in justified text.
Aligning content that will be rewrapped later, which discards the work entirely.

text-repeater.intro: Text Repeater repeats a string a set number of times with a separator of your choosing.
how: Enter the text to repeat.
Set the number of repetitions and the separator.
Copy the result.
uses: Generating test data of a specific length or row count.
Building a repeated pattern for a template or a placeholder.
Creating a separator line of a set width.
Producing repeated markup rows to paste into a document.
text-repeater.method_title: The separator is the useful part
method: Repetition alone is trivial. The separator is what makes the output usable, because it decides whether you get one long string, a list of lines, or a comma-separated series ready to paste into code.

Choosing a newline gives you rows. Choosing a comma gives you an array body. Choosing an empty separator gives you a solid block, which is what you want for building a fixed-width rule or padding test input.
mistakes: Generating an enormous repetition and pasting it somewhere that cannot handle it. Browsers and editors both struggle past a few megabytes.
Forgetting that a trailing separator is usually left on the end and may need removing.

csv-viewer.intro: CSV Viewer renders pasted CSV as a formatted, sortable table. It supports comma, tab, semicolon, pipe and custom delimiters, and can treat the first row as a header.
how: Paste your CSV data.
Choose the delimiter, or enter a custom one.
Tick First row is header if it applies.
Press Render Table, then click column headers to sort.
csv-viewer.method_title: Why CSV is less standard than it sounds
method: RFC 4180 describes the common format, but plenty of real files ignore it. A field containing a comma has to be wrapped in double quotes, and a field containing a double quote has to double it up. Files produced by hand or by naive code routinely get this wrong.

The delimiter itself is not fixed either. Many European locales export with semicolons, because the comma is already in use as the decimal separator. That is why a spreadsheet exported in one country can arrive as a single unparsed column in another.
uses: Reading a CSV file without opening a spreadsheet application.
Checking an export looks right before importing it somewhere.
Sorting a data set quickly to spot outliers.
Inspecting data with an unusual delimiter that a spreadsheet guesses wrongly.
mistakes: Choosing the wrong delimiter and getting one wide column, which usually means the file is semicolon-separated.
Assuming quoted fields will always parse. Malformed quoting is common and shifts every subsequent column.
Forgetting the header setting, which either loses the first row of data or labels columns with a data row.
notes: Data is parsed in your browser and never uploaded anywhere.

compound-interest.intro: Compound Interest Calculator projects what a starting balance grows to over time, with regular monthly contributions, a choice of compounding frequency, a growth chart and a year-by-year breakdown.
how: Enter your starting principal and annual interest rate.
Set the time period and how often interest compounds: annually, quarterly, monthly or daily.
Add a monthly contribution if you plan to keep paying in.
Read the projection and the year-by-year table.
compound-interest.method_title: Why compounding pulls away from simple interest
method: Simple interest pays only on the original principal. Compound interest pays on the principal plus everything it has already earned, so each period starts from a larger base. That is why the curve bends upward instead of running straight.

Compounding frequency matters less than people expect. Going from annual to monthly compounding at the same rate adds a fraction of a percent. What actually dominates the result is the rate, the time, and how much you keep adding.

example.setup: Using the values the calculator loads with:
example.result: About $137,000. Of that, $58,000 is money you put in and roughly $79,000 is growth. The growth overtakes the contributions somewhere around year twelve.

uses: Projecting a retirement or index fund balance over a long horizon.
Seeing what raising a monthly contribution by $50 does over twenty years.
Comparing two savings rates over the same period.
Understanding why starting five years earlier beats contributing more later.
mistakes: Using a nominal return and forgetting inflation. A 7% return with 3% inflation is about 4% in real buying power.
Assuming a steady rate. Real markets do not deliver 7% every year, and the order of good and bad years matters once you start withdrawing.
Confusing APR with APY. APY already includes compounding, APR does not.
notes: This is a projection tool, not financial advice. Past returns do not predict future ones.

debt-snowball.intro: Debt Snowball Calculator plans a payoff schedule across all your debts, using either the snowball method or the avalanche method, and shows what an extra monthly payment does to your payoff date and total interest.
how: Add each debt with its name, balance, minimum payment and APR.
Enter the extra amount you can put toward debt each month.
Switch between Snowball and Avalanche to compare.
Read the payoff order, the date, and the total interest for each strategy.
method: Both methods pay the minimum on everything and throw all spare money at one debt. They differ only in which one. Snowball targets the smallest balance first. Avalanche targets the highest interest rate first.

Avalanche always costs less in total interest, sometimes by a lot. Snowball clears individual debts sooner, which produces visible wins early and is why studies of real behaviour find people stick with it more often. The best method is the one you will actually finish, so compare both and be honest about which you will keep doing in month fourteen.

example.setup: The debt the calculator loads with:
example.result: Paying $175 instead of $75 clears the card in well under half the time and cuts the interest paid dramatically, because at 20% APR most of a minimum payment is interest.

uses: Choosing between snowball and avalanche with your real numbers instead of arguing about it in the abstract.
Seeing what an extra $50 a month actually buys in months saved.
Getting a concrete payoff date rather than an open-ended feeling of debt.
Deciding which card to attack first.
mistakes: Paying minimums on everything and nothing extra. Minimum payments on a high-APR card are designed to keep the balance alive for years.
Ignoring the APR entirely. A 6% car loan and a 24% credit card are not the same problem.
Adding new debt while paying off old debt, which resets the whole plan.
notes: A planning tool, not financial advice. Check any consolidation or refinancing offer against these figures before accepting it.

savings-goal-planner.intro: Savings Goal Planner answers the two questions people actually have about a savings target: how long it will take at your current rate, or how much you need to save monthly to hit a deadline. Interest is included.
how: Enter your goal amount and what you have saved already.
For a timeline, enter your monthly contribution and press How long?
For a required amount, enter your target months and press How much per month?
Add your account's APY so interest is counted.
method: Each month your balance earns interest and you add a contribution, so the balance grows from both directions. Over short horizons the interest is small. Over several years it starts to carry real weight.
At current savings account rates the effect is modest but not nothing, and it is the difference between hitting a goal a month or two early and hitting it late.

example.setup: The defaults, saving toward $10,000:
example.result: About 20 months. Without any interest the same plan takes about 22, so the account is worth roughly two months.

uses: Setting a realistic date for an emergency fund or a down payment.
Working out the monthly figure needed to hit a fixed deadline.
Comparing what a higher-yield account actually saves you in time.
Checking whether a savings goal is achievable before committing to it.
mistakes: Ignoring the difference between APY and the advertised rate. APY is the one that includes compounding.
Planning to the last dollar with no slack. Goals that assume zero unexpected expenses fail on the first unexpected expense.
Forgetting that promotional rates expire, often after twelve months.
notes: Projections only, not financial advice. Rates change and are not guaranteed.

budget-planner.intro: Budget Planner lets you add your own income and expense categories and shows the totals, the balance left over, and how your spending is distributed.
how: Add each income source with its monthly amount.
Add each expense category.
Read the totals and the remaining balance.
method: A widely used starting framework is 50/30/20: roughly half of take-home pay to needs (housing, food, transport, minimum debt payments), thirty percent to wants, twenty percent to savings and extra debt repayment.

It is a benchmark rather than a rule, and it breaks in expensive housing markets where rent alone can exceed fifty percent. Its real value is as a diagnostic: if needs are at seventy percent, the problem is structural and no amount of trimming the wants column will fix it.
uses: Seeing where the money actually goes rather than estimating.
Finding the categories that have quietly grown.
Checking whether a planned expense fits before committing to it.
Working out how much is genuinely available for savings or debt.
mistakes: Forgetting irregular expenses. Insurance, car registration and annual subscriptions wreck budgets built only from monthly bills.
Budgeting from gross pay instead of take-home. Only what lands in the account is spendable.
Building a budget and never revisiting it. It reflects one month's assumptions and those change.
notes: Everything stays in your browser. Nothing is uploaded or stored on a server.

tax-bracket.intro: Tax Bracket Calculator works out US federal income tax bracket by bracket for any income and filing status, and shows both the marginal rate and the effective rate. The difference between those two is the point of the tool.
how: Enter your income.
Choose your filing status: single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, or head of household.
Pick the tax year.
Read the tax owed per bracket, plus your marginal and effective rates.
tax-bracket.method_title: Marginal is not what you pay on everything
method: US federal income tax is progressive, which means the brackets apply to slices of income rather than all of it. Being in the 22% bracket does not mean 22% of your income goes to federal tax. It means the portion above that bracket's threshold is taxed at 22%, while the income below it is taxed at 10% and 12%.

Your effective rate is total tax divided by total income, and it is always lower than your marginal rate. This is why the widespread belief that a raise can leave you worse off is false: only the dollars above the threshold are taxed at the higher rate.

example.setup: Tax on $75,000 of taxable income, filing single:
example.result: About $11,553 total. Marginal rate 22%, but effective rate roughly 15.4%.

uses: Understanding what a raise actually costs you in tax.
Estimating federal tax before filing.
Comparing filing statuses.
Working out whether a pre-tax contribution is worth making, which depends on your marginal rate.
mistakes: Believing a raise into a higher bracket can reduce take-home pay. It cannot, under a progressive system.
Confusing gross income with taxable income. Deductions come off first, and the standard deduction alone is substantial.
Forgetting this is federal only. State income tax, FICA and local taxes are all separate.
notes: An estimate for federal income tax only, and not tax advice. It does not model credits, itemised deductions, capital gains, self-employment tax or state tax. Consult a tax professional for anything that matters.

inflation-calculator.intro: Inflation Calculator shows what an amount of money from one year is worth in another, using an annual inflation rate you can set yourself.
how: Enter the amount and the year it comes from.
Set the year you want to compare to.
Adjust the annual inflation rate if you want a different assumption.
Read the adjusted value.
method: Inflation compounds like interest. An amount is multiplied by one plus the rate, once for every year between the two dates. Over long spans that compounding produces figures that surprise people.

The rate you choose drives everything. US inflation has averaged somewhere near 3% over the long run, but individual years have ranged from negative to over 8%, so a single average smooths over periods that felt very different to live through.

example.setup: The default comparison:
example.result: About $2,081. You would need roughly twice as many dollars in 2024 to buy what $1,000 bought in 2000.

uses: Understanding whether a raise actually kept pace with the cost of living.
Comparing a historical price or salary to today's money.
Checking whether an investment return beat inflation in real terms.
Putting an old figure in a document into modern context.
mistakes: Treating the average rate as what you personally experienced. Housing, healthcare and education have risen far faster than the general index, and electronics have fallen.
Comparing nominal returns across decades without adjusting. A 5% return in a 9% inflation year is a real loss.
Assuming a single national figure applies to your city.
notes: Uses a flat annual rate that you set, not official year-by-year index data. Change the rate to model different assumptions.

roi-calculator.intro: ROI Calculator works out return on investment, total profit, and the annualized return, which is the number that actually lets you compare investments of different lengths.
how: Enter your initial investment and the final value.
Enter the duration in years.
Add any additional costs, which are subtracted from the return.
Read the total ROI and the annualized figure.
roi-calculator.method_title: Why annualized return is the number that matters
method: Total ROI is simply the gain divided by what you put in. It is easy to calculate and useless for comparison, because it says nothing about how long the money was tied up.

Annualized return solves that by expressing the result as a constant yearly rate. A 45% total return sounds impressive until you learn it took three years, at which point it is about 13% a year. Comparing a two-year investment to a ten-year one on total ROI alone will lead you to the wrong conclusion every time.

example.setup: The default figures:
example.result: $4,500 profit, 45% total ROI, and about 13.2% annualized.

uses: Comparing investments that ran for different lengths of time.
Evaluating a business project or a marketing spend.
Checking whether a return beat what an index fund would have done.
Including transaction costs and fees, which is where real returns quietly erode.
mistakes: Comparing total ROI across different time periods. It is the most common way to talk yourself into a worse investment.
Leaving out costs. Fees, commissions and taxes are the difference between the headline return and what you keep.
Ignoring risk. A 13% return from an index fund and a 13% return from a single speculative bet are not the same result.
notes: A calculation tool, not investment advice.

break-even-calculator.intro: Break-Even Calculator finds how many units you need to sell before you stop losing money, from your fixed costs, variable cost per unit and selling price. It also handles a target profit, and has presets for startup, retail and consulting shapes.
how: Enter your fixed costs: rent, salaries, software, anything that does not change with volume.
Enter the variable cost per unit and your selling price.
Add a target profit if you want the volume needed to reach it, not just to break even.
Try the Startup, Retail or Consulting presets to see typical shapes.
break-even-calculator.method_title: Contribution margin is the whole calculation
method: Every sale contributes its selling price minus its variable cost toward covering the fixed costs. That difference is the contribution margin, and break-even is simply fixed costs divided by it.

This is why raising price and cutting variable cost are so much more powerful than raising volume. A one dollar price rise adds a full dollar of contribution per unit, straight to the margin, while selling more units only adds one margin at a time.

example.setup: The default business:
example.result: 500 units to break even. To also make the $5,000 target profit you need 709 units, because ($12,000 + $5,000) / $24.

uses: Checking whether a business idea can work before committing money to it.
Working out the minimum volume a price point requires.
Seeing how much a price increase reduces the volume you need.
Deciding whether a fixed-cost commitment like a lease or a hire is supportable.
mistakes: Misclassifying costs. A cost that scales with sales is variable, not fixed, and putting it in the wrong column moves break-even substantially.
Forgetting your own salary. If the plan does not pay you, it has not broken even.
Treating break-even as the goal. It is the point where you stop losing money, not the point where the business works.

loan-comparison.intro: Loan Comparison puts two loans side by side, with different rates, terms, amounts or extra payments, and shows the monthly cost and the total cost of each.
how: Enter the amount, rate, term and any extra monthly payment for Loan A.
Do the same for Loan B.
Compare the monthly payments and, more importantly, the totals.
loan-comparison.method_title: Monthly payment is the wrong comparison
method: Lenders compete on monthly payment because it is the number borrowers react to, and it is the easiest number to make look good. Extending the term lowers the monthly payment on any loan while increasing what you pay overall.

Total cost over the life of the loan is the honest comparison. Compare monthly payment only when the two loans have identical terms, and even then check the total, because fees and rate differences show up there.

example.setup: The default comparison, same amount and term, 0.6 points of rate apart:
example.result: Roughly $7 a month, which looks trivial, but about $416 over the life of the loan.

uses: Comparing two real offers before signing.
Seeing what a rate difference is worth in dollars rather than percentage points.
Testing whether a shorter term is affordable.
Modelling what overpaying does to each option.
mistakes: Comparing loans with different terms on monthly payment. The longer one always looks cheaper and usually is not.
Ignoring fees. Origination and arrangement fees do not appear in the rate but do appear in what you pay.
Comparing an advertised rate to a quoted one. Advertised rates assume the best credit profile.

currency-converter.intro: Currency Converter converts between more than thirty world currencies using a built-in rate table, with a quick view of one US dollar against every supported currency.
how: Enter an amount.
Choose the source and target currencies, or use the swap button to reverse them.
Read the converted amount, or use the quick convert view for a full comparison.
currency-converter.method_title: Why exchange rates are never one number
method: There is no single true exchange rate. The mid-market rate is the midpoint between what buyers and sellers are offering, and it is the figure quoted in news reports. It is not the rate you will get.

Banks, card networks and exchange bureaux all add a margin, typically anywhere from under one percent to several percent, and some add a fixed fee as well. The mid-market rate is the benchmark to measure an offer against, not a prediction of what you will receive.
uses: Getting a quick sense of what a foreign price is worth.
Checking a quoted exchange rate against the benchmark to see the margin.
Comparing prices across countries when shopping online.
Estimating a travel budget.
mistakes: Expecting to receive the quoted rate. Every provider takes a margin somewhere.
Comparing providers on rate alone while ignoring a fixed transfer fee, which dominates on small amounts.
Using card conversion at the point of sale when offered the choice. Paying in the local currency is almost always cheaper than letting the terminal convert.
notes: Uses a built-in rate table rather than a live feed, so figures are indicative and will drift from the market. Check a live source before making a financial decision.

rule-of-72.intro: Rule of 72 tells you roughly how many years it takes to double your money at a given rate of return. Type a rate or drag the slider, with presets for typical savings, index and aggressive returns.
how: Type an annual return rate, or drag the slider anywhere from 0.1% to 30%.
Use the presets for common cases: savings at 3%, index at 7%, aggressive at 10%.
Read the years to double.
rule-of-72.method_title: Why 72, and where it stops working
method: Divide 72 by the annual percentage return and you get the approximate years to double. At 8% that is 9 years, and the true answer from the compounding formula is 9.01, so the shortcut is remarkably close.

The approximation is most accurate between about 6% and 10%. It drifts outside that band: at 2% the rule says 36 years and the real figure is 35, while at 20% the rule says 3.6 years and the real figure is closer to 3.8. It is a mental-arithmetic tool, not a precise calculation.

example.setup: Three common return rates:
example.result: The gap between 3% and 7% is not twice as fast, it is more than twice, which is the intuition the rule is good at delivering.

uses: Getting a fast sense of a return rate without a calculator.
Comparing the long-run impact of two rates in your head.
Understanding what inflation does, by applying the same rule to how fast prices double.
Explaining compounding to someone quickly.
mistakes: Using it for precise planning. It is an approximation and drifts at the extremes.
Applying it to volatile returns as though they were steady. Markets do not deliver the average every year.
Forgetting it works on inflation too. At 3% inflation, prices double in 24 years.
notes: A rule of thumb, not financial advice or a guarantee of any return.
